prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a negative antigen test to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the lumbar puncture.
Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ceftriaxone for 14 days for Streptococcus pneumoniae (ceftriaxone MIC <=0.5 mg/L), stopping vancomycin if it was added (NICE NG240).
Stop as-needed ibuprofen while he receives dexamethasone (additive gastrointestinal bleeding risk) and use paracetamol for headache.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in the diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

CT before lumbar puncture is not indicated: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Imaging here only delays the lumbar puncture.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

differential.key_features: The preceding upper respiratory infection, modest mixed pleocytosis, normal glucose ratio and negative Gram stain raise it; excluded by Streptococcus pneumoniae on CSF PCR and in CSF and blood cultures, with enterovirus and herpesviruses not detected.
Young adult with a daycare contact and uncertain meningococcal vaccine type; no rash; excluded by Neisseria meningitidis not detected on PCR and Streptococcus pneumoniae in CSF and blood.
Mild inattention, but no seizures, focal deficits or aphasia; HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on PCR.
Subacute course, lymphocytic CSF and very low glucose are absent; pneumococcus is identified.
Gradual headache after a viral prodrome, not thunderclap; CSF RBC 2 cells/microL and no xanthochromia.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Early bacterial meningitis can show a modest mixed pleocytosis with a normal glucose ratio; here the raised CSF lactate, the blood inflammatory markers, the multiplex PCR and the blood cultures carry the diagnosis.
Antigen detection is not among the WHO 2025 recommended tests and can be falsely negative, as here; a positive antigen result also needs culture or molecular confirmation.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram stain sensitivity is limited, reported at 85 per cent with wide confidence limits in WHO 2025, and a negative result does not exclude bacterial meningitis. Antigen detection may also be falsely negative, as here. Culture with susceptibility testing and multiplex PCR are the tests that establish the organism.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain and negative bacterial antigen test
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the index of suspicion for bacterial meningitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatraemia (sodium 130 mEq/L) is common in bacterial meningitis, often attributed to SIADH; it is monitored and corrected alongside treatment of the infection and does not explain the meningism, CSF pleocytosis or confusion.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

metadata.clinical_notes: This case represents a diagnostic puzzle where early bacterial meningitis presents with atypical CSF findings that initially mimic viral meningitis. The key diagnostic challenge is maintaining clinical suspicion for bacterial etiology despite ambiguous initial results.
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response
teaching_points: Always consider early bacterial meningitis when CSF shows mixed pleocytosis, even if Gram stain is negative
CSF lactate is a valuable discriminator between bacterial and viral meningitis
Do not delay empiric antibiotics for any reason when bacterial meningitis is on the differential
Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics to be maximally effective

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Daniel Kowalski is a 35-year-old right-handed high school mathematics teacher who presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of progressively worsening headache and neck stiffness. He reports that his symptoms began approximately five days ago with rhinorrhea, mild sore throat, and general malaise, which he attributed to catching the upper respiratory infection that had been circulating through his household after his daughter brought it home from daycare. He treated his symptoms with over-the-counter cold medications and continued working. Three days ago, he developed a bifrontal headache that he initially managed with ibuprofen 400 mg every six hours with partial relief. Over the past 48 hours, however, the headache has progressively intensified and become more diffuse, now described as a constant, pressure-like pain rated 7 out of 10 that worsens with movement and when bending forward. He notes that his neck has felt stiff since yesterday, which he initially attributed to sleeping in an awkward position. He reports subjective fevers and chills at home over the past two days, though his wife measured his temperature at 37.8 degrees Celsius yesterday evening. He denies rigors or documented high fevers. He endorses mild nausea without vomiting, decreased appetite, and significant fatigue. He took a sick day from work today and was encouraged to come to the emergency department by his wife after she noticed he seemed somewhat confused when he could not remember whether he had already taken his morning medications, an unusual lapse for him. He denies any rash, vision changes, seizures, focal weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, or problems with balance. He has not experienced any ear pain, sinus pressure beyond his initial cold symptoms, or dental problems. He has no history of recent head trauma, neurosurgical procedures, or lumbar punctures. His immunization history is up to date, including a meningococcal vaccine during college, though he is uncertain about its specific type. He has not traveled recently and has no known exposure to anyone with meningitis.
